title: From fork() to Fleet: Designing an Agent Sandbox Cloud — Abhishek Bhardwaj, OpenAI

summary: Abhishek Bhardwaj, working on RL and agent infrastructure at OpenAI, presents a first-principles exploration of agent sandbox cloud design. The talk begins by motivating why AI models need execution environments: large pre-trained models answer common questions well but struggle with verifiable problems like counting letters in "strawberry" or performing math, unless given tool calling capability. By allowing models to write and execute code, they can hill-climb toward correct answers on tasks with verifiable rewards, fundamental to both training and product deployment. On the training side, a harness parses model responses, executes requested code, and a grader judges correctness, feeding back into the weight update loop. The product side mirrors this minus the training loop—code must execute somewhere. Security is paramount: models may intentionally or unintentionally attempt root access or exploit kernel vulnerabilities, and in multi-tenant cloud environments, sandboxes must prevent cross-user data exfiltration. Bhardwaj notes the irony of agents running locally on laptops, predicting a future of persistent cloud agents. Research sandboxes prioritize throughput for many parallel rollouts; product sandboxes prioritize latency. Both require reliability and security. The talk outlines three pillars: runtime, persistence, and orchestration. The technical deep-dive covers Linux fundamentals: threads, system calls, processor rings (ring 0 kernel, ring 3 user mode), and two attack vectors: gaining root and kernel exploits. The simplest model—fork()/exec()—offers native performance but no security. Containers improve via namespaces and cgroups but remain native processes sharing the host kernel. seccomp filters reduce attack surface but create poor feedback loops for agent products. GVisor implements a user-space application kernel but chained two-step exploits can still reach the host kernel. Hardware virtualization provides the strongest boundary via VMX root/non-root modes. Modern Rust-based VMMs (CrosVM, Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor) define microVMs through memory safety, device jailing, smaller footprint, and faster boot. MicroVMs are orchestrated via APIs: a harness forks a VMM binary, calls create with root FS/kernel/CPU/memory, then start; the VMM calls into /dev/kvm. Trade-offs include performance overhead from VMX transitions, reactive memory reclaim via balloon drivers, and GPU access limitations. Bhardwaj strongly prefers security over performance, noting all sandboxing efforts eventually converge on VMs. The persistence pillar is motivated by agents needing durable storage. Three use cases: reliability via checkpointing, long-running tasks (Codex gold mode, multi-day sessions), and research via Monte Carlo tree search. Explicit persistence uses copy-on-write on XFS-like filesystems: a writable layer atop a base image, with FIE map identifying changed blocks, zipping diffs to cloud with async upload for fast snapshot returns. Always-on persistence uses NBD (Network Block Device) on top of GCS/S3 with a tiered block-level cache—in-cluster cache writing back to object storage—giving a performant POSIX-compliant filesystem inside the microVM. NFS is rejected as less performant and not POSIX-compliant. Fleet-level orchestration groups nodes into clusters across regions, with a control plane choosing clusters by region load and proximity to ChatGPT clusters, and per-cluster schedulers picking nodes by load. Low-latency creation strategies include pre-warming warm pools, just-in-time memory snapshot restoration in milliseconds, and hybrid approaches trading idle resource consumption against startup speed. Snapshot lineage-aware scheduling routes sandbox creation to nodes already holding the most snapshot layers, minimizing download time. Bhardwaj identifies storage as the next major unlock for agent capabilities.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and motivation
sections.summary: Abhishek introduces himself as working on RL and agent infrastructure at OpenAI, covering infra for reinforcement learning and running untrusted code securely in ChatGPT and Codex Web. The talk is a first-principles exploration of agent sandbox cloud design, described as a spiritual sequel to his previous talk on building AI sandboxes from scratch.

sections.title: Why AI models need tools and execution environments
sections.summary: Explains that pre-trained models answer common questions well but fail on verifiable problems like counting letters in 'strawberry' because training data lacks sufficient examples. The key unlock was giving models tool calling and code execution capability, enabling hill-climbing on tasks with verifiable rewards. Describes the training loop: harness parses model responses, executes requested code, grader judges correctness, and weights update accordingly.

sections.title: Product-side challenges and security
sections.summary: The product side mirrors training minus the training loop—code executes on laptops or cloud nodes. Security concerns include models intentionally or unintentionally attempting root access or kernel exploits. In multi-tenant clouds, sandboxes must prevent cross-user data exfiltration. Abhishek notes the irony of agents running locally on laptops, predicting persistent cloud agents as the future.

sections.title: Research vs. product sandbox requirements
sections.summary: Research sandboxes optimize for throughput with many parallel rollouts, while product sandboxes prioritize latency—slow execution causes user churn. Both require reliability (GPU tokens are expensive) and security (preventing infrastructure attacks, model weight exfiltration, and cross-user data theft).

sections.title: Three pillars overview
sections.summary: Introduces the three pillars of sandbox cloud design: runtime (secure single-node execution), persistence (durable storage enabling agents as true knowledge workers), and orchestration (scaling to ChatGPT and Codex scale).

sections.title: Linux execution first principles
sections.summary: Covers Linux fundamentals: threads as smallest execution unit, kernel providing privileged access via system calls, and processor rings (ring 0 for kernel mode, ring 3 for user mode). Two attack vectors exist: gaining root (still ring 3 but highest user privilege, can read SSH keys) and kernel exploits (ring 0, catastrophic).

sections.title: fork() and exec model
sections.summary: The simplest execution model: an API server forks a process and execs the tool for each call. It offers native performance as the fastest solution, but has critical problems: the forked process can directly attack the kernel, and unbounded forking creates noisy neighbor issues.

sections.title: Containers: namespaces and cgroups
sections.summary: Containers rely on namespaces for resource isolation (PID, mount, network) and cgroups for controlling resource consumption. However, containers remain native processes sharing the host kernel—processes can still exploit the kernel boundary to get root or kernel exploits, enabling cross-sandbox data exfiltration.

sections.title: seccomp and container security limitations
sections.summary: seccomp filters reduce the kernel attack surface by controlling which system calls a container can invoke. However, you often don't know beforehand what system calls an agent might need, creating a poor feedback loop. For agent products wanting magical experiences, this restrictiveness is problematic.

sections.title: GVisor: user-space application kernel
sections.summary: GVisor addresses the attack surface problem by implementing many system calls in user space via a 'sentry' and a 'gofer' daemon. However, the sentry and gofer still run on the host kernel, making chained two-step exploits possible: first exploit the sentry/gofer, then exploit the host kernel.

sections.title: Hardware-level virtualization
sections.summary: Linux provides hardware-powered virtualization at the CPU level. The guest kernel runs in ring 0 but in VMX non-root mode, while the host/hypervisor runs in VMX root mode. This guarantees that even if an attacker gets root in the guest, the host remains protected. The trade-off is a performance penalty on VMX transitions.

sections.title: VMMs and KVM architecture
sections.summary: VMMs like QEMU interface with /dev/kvm. The VMM sets up guest memory, root filesystem, and devices. Paravirtualization uses virtio drivers—guest drivers aware they're in a VM—communicating via PCI devices for better performance.

sections.title: Modern Rust-based VMMs and microVMs
sections.summary: A seismic shift occurred with Rust-based VMMs. CrosVM was first, built by Google for Chromebooks. Firecracker forked from CrosVM for AWS Lambda; Cloud Hypervisor is a community VMM. 'microVM' refers to VMM properties (smaller memory footprint, faster boot), not guest contents.

sections.title: Orchestrating microVMs via APIs
sections.summary: Explains how to start a microVM: the harness forks a Cloud Hypervisor binary process, which exposes an API over a Unix domain socket. The harness calls create with root FS, kernel, CPU, and memory, then calls start. The VMM calls into /dev/kvm to start the guest. Inside the sandbox, PID 1 exposes an API server for external communication via Vsock (guest-host socket) or the node's IP stack.

sections.title: Trade-offs of microVMs
sections.summary: MicroVMs provide excellent hardware-level isolation but with trade-offs. Attacking the host requires compromising the KVM stack and then a device—much harder, but possible. Devices can be jailed with seccomp for granular security. Performance overhead comes from VMX root/non-root transitions. Memory sharing is reactive via balloon driver. GPU access is limited: virtio GPU provides high-level graphics only, VFIO enables direct metal access but is single-tenant only. Bhardwaj strongly prefers security over performance, noting the 'seven stages of grief' in sandboxing—everyone eventually wants a VM after trying containers, GVisor, and V8s.

sections.title: The need for persistent storage
sections.summary: Motivates persistence by analogy: giving an agent a computer without a disk means all work is lost when the laptop closes. Cloud agents currently face this problem. Tasks are becoming more complex and longer-horizon—presentations, entire GitHub repos created inside sandboxes. If a node dies or the model flakes, work is lost, wasting GPU tokens and harming user experience.

sections.title: Use cases for persistence
sections.summary: Persistence enables three capabilities: (1) Reliability and scale—periodic checkpointing allows restoring sandboxes on another node after failures, cluster upgrades, or A/B testing. (2) Long-running tasks—Codex gold mode runs for days (speaker's record: 3 days). (3) Research—harnesses can checkpoint sandbox state for Monte Carlo tree search, enabling backtracking and multi-day rollouts.

sections.title: Design choices for disk snapshotting
sections.summary: Snapshotting at ChatGPT/Codex scale requires incremental snapshotting (only diffs between snapshots) to avoid saving gigabytes per turn. The API must be fast and cheap for rapid exploration, and restoration must be equally fast. Two paradigms: always-on vs explicit. Design choices include incremental vs full, entire root FS vs selective folders, and file-system-level vs block-level snapshotting.

sections.title: Linux block storage and persistence implementations
sections.summary: Explains Linux storage from first principles: disks are block devices with logical blocks; file systems map files to blocks via inodes; firmware maps logical blocks to sectors. Block device abstraction inside microVMs is far more efficient than shared-folder approaches because the guest can use caches and only exits on actual block device access.

sections.title: Explicit persistence with copy-on-write
sections.summary: Implements explicit persistence using copy-on-write on XFS-like filesystems. A base image (Codex or ChatGPT base image) has a zero-copy writable layer on top. Writes modify blocks in this layer. FIE map identifies which blocks and ranges have changed. Changed blocks are zipped and uploaded to cloud. A key optimization: the snapshot API returns immediately while upload happens asynchronously in the background. Restoration downloads the diff artifact, identifies changed extents, applies them on top of the base image, and restarts the microVM with exact block-level state.

sections.title: Always-on persistence with NBD and tiered caching
sections.summary: Always-on persistence avoids NFS (less performant, not POSIX-compliant) by writing a filesystem on top of GCS/S3/durable block storage using NBD (Network Block Device). Inside the sandbox, a block device is exposed with a tiered cache: blocks are first persisted to an in-cluster cache, which writes back to object storage. This gives a performant, POSIX-compliant filesystem inside the microVM. Bhardwaj emphasizes storage as the next major unlock for agent capabilities.

sections.title: Fleet-level orchestration
sections.summary: Addresses scaling beyond single nodes. Nodes are grouped into clusters spread across regions. A top-level control plane chooses a cluster based on region load and proximity to ChatGPT clusters for low-latency harness access. Within each cluster, a scheduler selects nodes based on load and health. Low latency and reliability remain key North Stars.

sections.title: Low-latency sandbox creation strategies
sections.summary: Three strategies for low-latency creation: (1) Pre-warming warm pools—pre-create sandboxes and pick one, trading idle CPU/memory consumption. (2) Memory snapshots—save guest memory and just-in-time start in milliseconds as requests arrive. (3) Hybrid—use warm pools but grow them from memory snapshots, getting best of both worlds. Trade-off is between warm pool idle resource consumption and memory snapshot approaches.

sections.title: Snapshot lineage-aware scheduling and conclusion
sections.summary: Snapshot lineage (multiple layers of diffs) enables smarter orchestration. When restoring a sandbox requiring multiple snapshot layers, the scheduler scores nodes by how many layers they already have cached—routing to the node with the most layers to minimize downloads. Bhardwaj concludes by emphasizing storage as the next unlock, encouraging the audience to think about what they can snapshot and restore fast to enable failure recovery and Monte Carlo search.

limitations: fork()/exec() model has no security isolation, no resource control, and risk of noisy neighbor problems from unbounded forking
Containers still share the host kernel—processes can exploit the kernel boundary to get root or kernel exploits, enabling cross-sandbox data exfiltration
seccomp filters create poor feedback loops—blocking unknown system calls restricts agent capabilities, requiring constant filter adjustments
GVisor's sentry and gofer still run on the host kernel, making chained two-step exploits possible to eventually reach the host kernel
Hardware virtualization incurs a performance penalty every time the CPU switches between VMX root and non-root modes
Memory sharing with microVMs is reactive—balloon driver requires asking the guest to give back memory, cannot immediately reclaim or claim memory
virtio GPU provides only high-level graphics library access, not full GPU compute; VFIO enables direct metal access but is single-tenant only, unsuitable for multi-tenant
Shared-folder storage inside microVMs is inefficient due to VM exiting at every filesystem operation
Full snapshotting at every turn would bankrupt the company and be a slow experience
QEMU has significant bloat—supports many architectures and devices, is written in C, and historically suffered escape attacks targeting C-written devices
NFS is not as performant and is not POSIX-compliant, making it less suitable for agent sandboxes
Warm pool consumes CPU and memory in idle state, creating a trade-off against low-latency startup
quantitativeClaims: 3 days is the speaker's record for running a Codex gold mode task
People are doing longer and longer tasks, a trend expected to continue in the cloud
Memory snapshot restoration can start a microVM in milliseconds as the request comes in
